Prior to the experiment, participants were given the LEAP-Q to assess their language history and background, including current exposure to languages in different contexts.  One that was of particular interest in bilinguals was current exposure to Mandarin radio and music, which is one of the only passive, auditory receptive (not productive) factors, since the basis of the task was an auditory receptive one.  Participants’ self-rated exposure to Mandarin radio and music scores were factored into a 2×3×2 ANCOVA parallel to the ANOVA previously run.  From this, a significant interaction was found, F(1,37) = 8.910, p = .005, as well as a main effect of group, F(1,37) = 6.292, p = .017, with bilinguals performing slower than monolinguals across all tasks.  A 2×3 ANCOVA was also run between match/mismatch and the three reaction times with Mandarin radio and listening exposure scores factored in for bilingual participants.  Again, a strong interaction between match and mismatch conditions with the three reaction times was found, F(1,18) = 10.958, p = .004. When factoring this covariate into bilingual match vs. mismatch reaction time analyses, a marginally significant difference between the match and mismatch reaction times for both the first, F(1,18) = 4.020, p = .060, and third, F(1,18) = 3.738, p = .069, reaction times was found.

In the present research, the effect on a word recognition task of a supra-segmental feature, tone, was examined. More specifically, we examined whether the superimposition of Mandarin tones on English words affected how Mandarin-English bilinguals perceived those words.  Data analyses of word choice suggested that Mandarin-English bilingual speakers did not perform differently than monolingual English speakers in word choice when a Mandarin tone was superimposed on the word.  This was not consistent with our hypothesis, which predicted that the Mandarin tone would affect the word choice and lead to a greater number of word choices where the superimposed tone matched the tone of the homophone’s Mandarin translation.  This could be due to different reasons, including word frequency and current exposure to English and Mandarin.  Stimulus words were chosen to not differ in English word frequency between the two members of a homophone pair by checking frequencies on the CELEX lexical database.¹²  However, we were not able to control for Mandarin word frequency, which may have played an important role in how readily participants recalled the Mandarin translation of the English words.  The factor of current exposure to Mandarin and English, measured using the LEAP-Q,¹³  revealed that the bilingual participants, though balanced, were currently and on average exposed to English 72.6% of the time, while only exposed to Mandarin 24.6% of the time.  This greater exposure to English, along with the fact that the entire experiment was conducted in English, may have led to Mandarin being less active than English while the bilinguals were participating in the experiment.  This could be an explanation as to why bilinguals appeared to perform similarly to monolinguals at this lexical level of the experiment.

Though ultimate word choice did not appear to be affected by tone in bilinguals, there did appear to be an effect of superimposed tone on how bilinguals processed the English words, as evidenced by the reaction time data.  For monolingual participants’ reaction times, no significant differences were found between the time it took to recognize, write, and orally produce words that matched or mismatched the Mandarin tone presented. Bilinguals, on the other hand, showed differences in the time it took for them to match and to mismatch in all three reaction times, though only the third reaction time, oral sentence production, reached significance.  For the auditory recognition task (first reaction time) and written production task (second reaction time), bilinguals matched slower than they mismatched.  Results for the first reaction time did not reach significance, though Power Analyses suggest that with a slightly larger sample size, a significant result could be achieved.  The second reaction time showed no significant difference, which is most likely due to the large variability in different participants’ writing speed.  In contrast to the first and second reaction times, for the oral production task (third reaction time) in the experiment, bilinguals matched significantly more quickly than they mismatched.  These seemingly contradictory patterns might be explained by activation of similar and competing information across languages.
